\*\*PRISMA NMA Checklist of Items to Include When Reporting A Systematic
Review Involving a Network Meta-analysis\*\*

<td><strong>TITLE</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>

<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Title</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>1</td>
<td>Identify the report as a systematic review <em>incorporating a
network meta-analysis (or related form of meta-analysis).</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>ABSTRACT</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Structured summary</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>2</td>
<td><p>Provide a structured summary including, as applicable:</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Background:</strong> main objectives</p>
<p><strong>Methods:</strong> data sources; study eligibility criteria,
participants, and interventions; study appraisal; and <em>synthesis
methods, such as network meta-analysis.</em></p>
<p><strong>Results:</strong> number of studies and participants
identified; summary estimates with corresponding confidence/credible
intervals; <em>treatment rankings may also be discussed. Authors may
choose to summarize pairwise comparisons against a chosen treatment
included in their analyses for brevity.</em></p>
<p><strong>Discussion/Conclusions:</strong> limitations; conclusions and
implications of findings.</p>
<p><strong>Other:</strong> primary source of funding; systematic review
registration number with registry name.</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>INTRODUCTION</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Rationale</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>3</td>
<td>Describe the rationale for the review in the context of what is
already known<em>, including mention of why a network meta-analysis has
been conducted.</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Objectives</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>4</td>
<td>Provide an explicit statement of questions being addressed, with
reference to participants, interventions, comparisons, outcomes, and
study design (PICOS).</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>METHODS</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Protocol and registration</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>5</td>
<td>Indicate whether a review protocol exists and if and where it can be
accessed (e.g., Web address); and, if available, provide registration
information, including registration number.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Eligibility criteria</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>6</td>
<td>Specify study characteristics (e.g., PICOS, length of follow-up) and
report characteristics (e.g., years considered, language, publication
status) used as criteria for eligibility, giving rationale. <em>Clearly
describe eligible treatments included in the treatment network, and note
whether any have been clustered or merged into the same node (with
justification).</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Information sources</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>7</td>
<td>Describe all information sources (e.g., databases with dates of
coverage, contact with study authors to identify additional studies) in
the search and date last searched.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Search</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>8</td>
<td>Present full electronic search strategy for at least one database,
including any limits used, such that it could be repeated.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Study selection</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>9</td>
<td>State the process for selecting studies (i.e., screening,
eligibility, included in systematic review, and, if applicable, included
in the meta-analysis).</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Data collection process</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>10</td>
<td>Describe method of data extraction from reports (e.g., piloted
forms, independently, in duplicate) and any processes for obtaining and
confirming data from investigators.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Data items</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>11</td>
<td>List and define all variables for which data were sought (e.g.,
PICOS, funding sources) and any assumptions and simplifications
made.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p><strong>Geometry of the network</strong></p>
</blockquote></td>
<td><strong>S1</strong></td>
<td>Describe methods used to explore the geometry of the treatment
network under study and potential biases related to it. This should
include how the evidence base has been graphically summarized for
presentation, and what characteristics were compiled and used to
describe the evidence base to readers.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Risk of bias within individual studies</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>12</td>
<td>Describe methods used for assessing risk of bias of individual
studies (including specification of whether this was done at the study
or outcome level), and how this information is to be used in any data
synthesis.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Summary measures</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>13</td>
<td>State the principal summary measures (e.g., risk ratio, difference
in means). <em>Also describe the use of additional summary measures
assessed, such as treatment rankings and surface under the cumulative
ranking curve (SUCRA) values, as well as modified approaches used to
present summary findings from meta-analyses.</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Planned methods of analysis</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>14</td>
<td><p>Describe the methods of handling data and combining results of
studies for each network meta-analysis. This should include, but not be
limited to:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><em>Handling of multi-arm trials;</em></p></li>
<li><p><em>Selection of variance structure;</em></p></li>
<li><p><em>Selection of prior distributions in Bayesian analyses;
and</em></p></li>
<li><p><em>Assessment of model fit.</em></p></li>
</ul></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p><strong>Assessment of Inconsistency</strong></p>
</blockquote></td>
<td><strong>S2</strong></td>
<td>Describe the statistical methods used to evaluate the agreement of
direct and indirect evidence in the treatment network(s) studied.
Describe efforts taken to address its presence when found.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Risk of bias across studies</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>15</td>
<td>Specify any assessment of risk of bias that may affect the
cumulative evidence (e.g., publication bias, selective reporting within
studies).</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Additional analyses</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>16</td>
<td><p>Describe methods of additional analyses if done, indicating which
were pre-specified. This may include, but not be limited to, the
following:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Sensitivity or subgroup analyses;</p></li>
<li><p>Meta-regression analyses;</p></li>
<li><p><em>Alternative formulations of the treatment network;
and</em></p></li>
<li><p><em>Use of alternative prior distributions for Bayesian analyses
(if applicable).</em></p></li>
</ul></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>RESULTS†</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Study selection</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>17</td>
<td>Give numbers of studies screened, assessed for eligibility, and
included in the review, with reasons for exclusions at each stage,
ideally with a flow diagram.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p><strong>Presentation of network structure</strong></p>
</blockquote></td>
<td><strong>S3</strong></td>
<td>Provide a network graph of the included studies to enable
visualization of the geometry of the treatment network.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p><strong>Summary of network geometry</strong></p>
</blockquote></td>
<td><strong>S4</strong></td>
<td>Provide a brief overview of characteristics of the treatment
network. This may include commentary on the abundance of trials and
randomized patients for the different interventions and pairwise
comparisons in the network, gaps of evidence in the treatment network,
and potential biases reflected by the network structure.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Study characteristics</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>18</td>
<td>For each study, present characteristics for which data were
extracted (e.g., study size, PICOS, follow-up period) and provide the
citations.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Risk of bias within studies</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>19</td>
<td>Present data on risk of bias of each study and, if available, any
outcome level assessment.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Results of individual studies</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>20</td>
<td>For all outcomes considered (benefits or harms), present, for each
study: 1) simple summary data for each intervention group, and 2) effect
estimates and confidence intervals. <em>Modified approaches may be
needed to deal with information from larger networks.</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Synthesis of results</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>21</td>
<td>Present results of each meta-analysis done, including
confidence/credible intervals. <em>In larger networks, authors may focus
on comparisons versus a particular comparator (e.g. placebo or standard
care), with full findings presented in an appendix. League tables and
forest plots may be considered to summarize pairwise comparisons.</em>
If additional summary measures were explored (such as treatment
rankings), these should also be presented.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p><strong>Exploration for inconsistency</strong></p>
</blockquote></td>
<td><strong>S5</strong></td>
<td>Describe results from investigations of inconsistency. This may
include such information as measures of model fit to compare consistency
and inconsistency models, <em>P</em> values from statistical tests, or
summary of inconsistency estimates from different parts of the treatment
network.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Risk of bias across studies</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>22</td>
<td>Present results of any assessment of risk of bias across studies for
the evidence base being studied.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Results of additional analyses</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>23</td>
<td>Give results of additional analyses, if done (e.g., sensitivity or
subgroup analyses, meta-regression analyses<em>, alternative network
geometries studied, alternative choice of prior distributions for
Bayesian analyses,</em> and so forth).</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>DISCUSSION</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Summary of evidence</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>24</td>
<td>Summarize the main findings, including the strength of evidence for
each main outcome; consider their relevance to key groups (e.g.,
healthcare providers, users, and policy-makers).</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Limitations</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>25</td>
<td>Discuss limitations at study and outcome level (e.g., risk of bias),
and at review level (e.g., incomplete retrieval of identified research,
reporting bias). <em>Comment on the validity of the assumptions, such as
transitivity and consistency. Comment on any concerns regarding network
geometry (e.g., avoidance of certain comparisons).</em></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Conclusions</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>26</td>
<td>Provide a general interpretation of the results in the context of
other evidence, and implications for future research.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>FUNDING</strong></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><blockquote>
<p>Funding</p>
</blockquote></td>
<td>27</td>
<td>Describe sources of funding for the systematic review and other
support (e.g., supply of data); role of funders for the systematic
review. This should also include information regarding whether funding
has been received from manufacturers of treatments in the network and/or
whether some of the authors are content experts with professional
conflicts of interest that could affect use of treatments in the
network.</td>
<td></td>
</tr>

PICOS = population, intervention, comparators, outcomes, study design.
\\ Text in italics indicateS wording specific to reporting of network
meta-analyses that has been added to guidance from the PRISMA statement.
† Authors may wish to plan for use of appendices to present all relevant
information in full detail for items in this section. &gt; \*\*<u>Box.
Terminology: Reviews With Networks of Multiple &gt; Treatments</u>\*\*
&gt; &gt; Different terms have been used to identify systematic reviews
that &gt; incorporate a network of multiple treatment comparisons. A
brief &gt; overview of common terms follows. &gt; &gt; \*Indirect
treatment comparison:\* Comparison of 2 interventions for &gt; which
studies against a common comparator, such as placebo or a &gt; standard
treatment, are available (i.e., indirect information). The &gt; direct
treatment effects of each intervention against the common &gt;
comparator (i.e., treatment effects from a comparison of interventions
&gt; made within a study) may be used to estimate an indirect treatment
&gt; comparison between the 2 interventions (\*\*Appendix Figure 1,
A\*\*). An &gt; indirect treatment comparison (ITC) may also involve
multiple links. &gt; For example, in \*\*Appendix Figure 1, B\*\*,
treatments B and D may be &gt; compared indirectly on the basis of
studies encompassing comparisons &gt; of B versus C, A versus C, and A
versus D. &gt; &gt; \*Network meta-analysis\* or \*mixed treatment
comparison\*: These terms, &gt; which are often used interchangeably,
refer to situations involving &gt; the simultaneous comparison of 3 or
more interventions. Any network of &gt; treatments consisting of
strictly unclosed loops can be thought of as &gt; a series of ITCs
(\*\*Appendix Figure 1, A and B\*\*). In mixed treatment &gt;
comparisons, both direct and indirect information is available to &gt;
inform the effect size estimates for at least some of the comparisons;
&gt; visually, this is shown by closed loops in a network graph
(\*\*Appendix &gt; Figure 1, C\*\*). Closed loops are not required to be
present for every &gt; comparison under study. "Network meta-analysis"
is an inclusive term &gt; that incorporates the scenarios of both
indirect and mixed treatment &gt; comparisons. &gt; &gt; \*Network
geometry evaluation:\* The description of characteristics of &gt; the
network of interventions, which may include use of numerical &gt;
summary statistics. This does not involve quantitative synthesis to &gt;
compare treatments. This evaluation describes the current evidence &gt;
available for the competing interventions to identify gaps and &gt;
potential bias. Network geometry is described further in \*\*Appendix
&gt; Box 4\*\*. &gt; &gt; \*\*<u>Appendix Box 1. The Assumption of
Transitivity for Network &gt; Meta-Analysis</u>\*\* &gt; &gt; Methods
for indirect treatment comparisons and network meta-analysis &gt; enable
learning about the relative treatment effects of, for example, &gt;
treatments A and B through use of studies where these interventions &gt;
are compared against a common therapy, C. &gt; &gt; When planning a
network meta-analysis, it is important to assess &gt; patient and study
characteristics across the studies that compare &gt; pairs of
treatments. These characteristics are commonly referred to as &gt;
\*effect modifiers\* and include traits such as average patient age,
&gt; gender distribution, disease severity, and a wide range of other
&gt; plausible features. &gt; &gt; For network meta-analysis to produce
valid results, it is important &gt; that the distribution of effect
modifiers is similar, for example, &gt; across studies of A versus B and
A versus C. This balance increases &gt; the plausibility of reliable
findings from an indirect comparison of B &gt; versus C through the
common comparator A. When this balance is &gt; present, the assumption
of transitivity can be judged to hold. &gt; &gt; Authors of network
meta-analyses should present systematic (and even &gt; tabulated)
information regarding patient and study characteristics &gt; whenever
available. This information helps readers to empirically &gt; evaluate
the validity of the assumption of transitivity by reviewing &gt; the
distribution of potential effect modifiers across trials. &gt; &gt;
\*\*<u>Appendix Box 2. Differences in Approach to Fitting Network &gt;
Meta-Analyses</u>\*\* &gt; &gt; Network meta-analysis can be performed
within either a frequentist or &gt; a Bayesian framework. Frequentist
and Bayesian approaches to &gt; statistics differ in their definitions
of probability. Thus far, the &gt; majority of published network
meta-analyses have used a Bayesian &gt; approach. &gt; &gt; Bayesian
analyses return the posterior probability distribution of all &gt; the
model parameters given the data and prior beliefs (e.g., from &gt;
external information) about the values of the parameters. They fully
&gt; encapsulate the uncertainty in the parameter of interest and thus
can &gt; make direct probability statements about these parameters
(e.g., the &gt; probability that one intervention is superior to
another). &gt; &gt; Frequentist analyses calculate the probability that
the observed data &gt; would have occurred under their sampling
distribution for hypothesized &gt; values of the parameters. This
approach to parameter estimation is &gt; more indirect than the Bayesian
approach. &gt; &gt; Bayesian methods have been criticized for their
perceived complexity &gt; and the potential for subjectivity to be
introduced by choice of a &gt; prior distribution that may affect study
findings. Others argue that &gt; explicit use of a prior distribution
makes transparent how individuals &gt; can interpret the same data
differently. Despite these challenges, &gt; Bayesian methods offer
considerable flexibility for statistical &gt; modeling. &gt; &gt;
In-depth introductions to Bayesian methods and discussion of these and
&gt; other issues can be found elsewhere. &gt; &gt; \*\*<u>Appendix Box
3. Network Meta-Analysis and Assessment of &gt; Consistency</u>\*\* &gt;
&gt; Network meta-analysis often involves the combination of direct and
&gt; indirect evidence. In the simplest case, we wish to compare
treatments &gt; A and B and have 2 sources of information: direct
evidence via studies &gt; comparing A versus B, and indirect evidence
via groups of studies &gt; comparing A and B with a common intervention,
C. Together, this &gt; evidence forms a closed loop, ABC. &gt; &gt;
Direct and indirect evidence for a comparison of interventions should
&gt; be combined only when their findings are similar in magnitude and
&gt; interpretation. For example, for a comparison of mortality rates
&gt; between A and B, an odds ratio determined from studies of A versus
B &gt; should be similar to the odds ratio comparing A versus B
estimated &gt; indirectly based on studies of A versus C and B versus C.
This &gt; assumption of comparability of direct and indirect evidence is
&gt; referred to as \*consistency\* of treatment effects. &gt; &gt; When
a treatment network contains a closed loop of interventions, it &gt; is
possible to examine statistically whether there is agreement &gt;
between the direct and indirect estimates of intervention effect. &gt;
&gt; Different methods to evaluate potential differences in relative
&gt; treatment effects estimated by direct and indirect comparisons are
&gt; grouped as \*local approaches\* and \*global approaches.\* Local
&gt; approaches (e.g., the Bucher method or the node-splitting method)
&gt; assess the presence of inconsistency for a particular pairwise &gt;
comparison in the network, whereas global approaches (e.g., &gt;
inconsistency models, \*I\*<sup>2</sup> measure for inconsistency) &gt;
consider the potential for inconsistency in the network as a whole. &gt;
&gt; Tests for inconsistency can have limited power to detect a true
&gt; difference between direct and indirect evidence. When multiple
loops &gt; are being tested for inconsistency, one or a few may show
&gt; inconsistency simply by chance. Further discussions of consistency
and &gt; related concepts are available elsewhere. &gt; &gt;
Inconsistency in a treatment network can indicate lack of transitivity
&gt; (see \*\*Appendix Box 1\*\*). &gt; &gt; \*\*<u>Appendix Box 4.
Network Geometry and Considerations for &gt; Bias</u>\*\* &gt; &gt; The
term \*network geometry\* is used to refer to the architecture of &gt;
the treatment comparisons that have been made for the condition under
&gt; study. This includes what treatments are involved in the
comparisons &gt; in a network, in what abundance they are present, the
respective &gt; numbers of patients randomly assigned to each treatment,
and whether &gt; particular treatments and comparisons may have been
preferred or &gt; avoided. &gt; &gt; Networks may take on different
shapes. Poorly connected networks &gt; depend extensively on indirect
comparisons. Meta-analyses of such &gt; networks may be less reliable
than those from networks where most &gt; treatments have been compared
against each other. &gt; &gt; Qualitative description of network
geometry should be provided and &gt; accompanied by a network graph.
Quantitative metrics assessing &gt; features of network geometry, such
as \*diversity\* (related to the &gt; number of treatments assessed and
the balance of evidence among them), &gt; \*co-occurrence\* (related to
whether comparisons between certain &gt; treatments are more or less
common), and \*homophily\* (related to the &gt; extent of comparisons
between treatments in the same class versus &gt; competing classes), can
also be mentioned. &gt; &gt; Although common, established steps for
reviewing network geometry do &gt; not yet exist, however examples of
in-depth evaluations have been &gt; described related to treatments for
tropical diseases and basal cell &gt; carcinoma and may be of interest
to readers. An example based on 75 &gt; trials of treatments for
pulmonary arterial hypertension (\*\*Appendix &gt; Figure 3\*\*)
suggests that head-to-head studies of active therapies may &gt; prove
useful to further strengthen confidence in interpretation of &gt;
summary estimates of treatment comparisons. &gt; &gt; \*\*<u>Appendix
Box 5. Probabilities and Rankings in Network &gt; Meta-Analysis</u>\*\*
&gt; &gt; Systematic reviews incorporating network meta-analyses can
provide &gt; information about the hierarchy of competing interventions
in terms of &gt; treatment rankings. &gt; &gt; The term \*treatment
ranking probabilities\* refers to the probabilities &gt; estimated for
each treatment in a network of achieving a particular &gt; placement in
an ordering of treatment effects from best to worst. A &gt; network of
10 treatments provides a total of 100 ranking &gt; probabilities—that
is, for each intervention, the chance of being &gt; ranked first,
second, third, fourth, fifth, and so forth). &gt; &gt; Several
techniques are feasible to summarize relative rankings, and &gt; include
graphical tools as well as different approaches for estimating &gt;
ranking probabilities. \*\*Appendix Figure 6\*\* shows 2 approaches to
&gt; presenting such information, on the basis of a comparison of
adjuvant &gt; interventions for resected pancreatic adenocarcinoma. &gt;
&gt; Robust reporting of rankings also includes specifying median ranks
&gt; with uncertainty intervals, cumulative probability curves, and the
&gt; surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA) curve. &gt; &gt;
Rankings can be reported along with corresponding estimates of &gt;
pairwise comparisons between interventions. Rankings should be &gt;
reported with probability estimates to minimize misinterpretation from
&gt; focusing too much on the most likely rank. &gt; &gt; Rankings may
exaggerate small differences in relative effects, &gt; especially if
they are based on limited information. An objective &gt; assessment of
the strength of information in the network and the &gt; magnitude of
absolute benefits should accompany rankings to minimize &gt; potential
biases. \*\*<u>Appendix Figure 1A-1C</u>\*\*
